(1) the brain responses to words with strong semantic association are larger than to words with weaker association, (2) the semantic association is reflected by early brain responses, and (3) the brain responses for words from different categories are different.

the early stages of visual word processing.

the neural basis of human language processing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain responses to words with strong multimodality associations were stronger and faster than to words with weak multimodality associations.

the brain is able to extract the semantic information from the incoming word stimuli at an early processing stage, and that this information is processed before the grammatical category of the word is determined.
semantic information is processed in a highly distributed manner and that it is available to the language system at a very early stage in the processing stream.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found that words with strong multimodality associations elicit stronger neuromagnetic brain activity than other words.
the human brain can process the meaning of individual words in a very short time.
the brain is capable of recognizing words in a highly parallel fashion, with the meaning of a word being processed at least as fast as its grammatical category.
The main takeaway from our work is that
semantic processing of a word is a highly dynamic process that starts very early, before the word is recognized as a word.
the brain is able to process the meaning of words before the grammatical category of the word has been determined.
the brain can distinguish between words with different meanings as early as 100 ms after stimulus onset, and this difference is reflected in the strength of the neuromagnetic brain response.
